chapters.title: Let's go back to our first love. Let's put the spotlight back where it belongs.
We cannot transmit purity to others if we live ourselves…
Let us pray together so that this word takes root in our lives:

segments.text: Introduction
Today our basic text is found in the book of Revelation, chapter 2, verses 1-7:

“Write to the angel of the church in Ephesus: This is what he who holds the seven stars in his right hand says, who walks among the seven golden lampstands: I know your works and your labor and your patience. I know you can't stand bad guys; that you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and that you have found them liars; that you have perseverance, and have suffered for my name's sake, and have not grown weary.

But what I have against you is that you abandoned your first love. Remember therefore from whence you have fallen, repent, and do your first works; if not, I will come to you, and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent. Yet you have this, that you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, works which I also hate.
Let him who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches: To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God. »
Beloved, the message I would like to share with you today is simple, but absolutely profound: Let us return to our first love.
1. The illusion of works without love

This phrase, “let's return to our first love”, we can hear it often, to the point that it becomes banal. But today I invite you to stop for a moment. Remember your first moments of faith. Remember that first moment when you truly encountered the Lord. Remember this fire that animated you, this intense thirst that consumed you.
Remember your first steps. Fresh steps, steps that were not calculated. Steps that were purely motivated by love and the desire to serve the One who redeemed us. Selfless and pure steps.
The text begins: “Write to the church in Ephesus: I know your works. » It is a striking truth: we can have works while having abandoned our first love.

The Lord said: “I know that you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not. » You can have this ease of discerning who is telling the truth and who is not, without being in the truth yourself. You can easily judge whether someone serves God well or badly, without being a good servant yourself.

The Lord adds: “Yet you have this, that you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, whom I also hate. » But what are the works of the Nicolaitans? It is this subtle and dangerous message that makes you believe that, just because you have grace, you can live in disorder. It's making you believe that God loves you so much that you can behave any way you want.
Let me tell you this: grace is not a passport to disorder. Rather, grace is a supernatural capacity to live holiness.
The works of the Nicolaitans involve twisting the Word of God by using the Word itself, taking verses out of context to justify compromise.
2. When service replaces the Lord

The Lord tells us: “I know your works. » Do you heal the sick? He knows your works. Do you preach the word eloquently? He knows your works. “But what I have against you is that you abandoned your first love. »
Works do not justify everything. The big trap is that service can end up replacing the Lord. Often the work becomes more important to you than the God of the work.

Ask yourself: does your heart always beat for the One you serve, or does it beat only for the service you do for Him? Does your heart still desire His presence, or is it simply seeking the desire to rule, to gain authority, to be seen, and to be first?

Before you found success or took on responsibility, you had no problem being pushed back, or sitting on the ground. The main thing for you was to love. You weren't the star; He was the star. But today, have you become the star of your own ministry?
Let's go back to our first love. Let's put the spotlight back where it belongs.

There is a formidable trap in ministry. The trap is believing that the ministry is more important than the Lord of the ministry. Let's put God back in His rightful place. The Church is not one man's church. As long as it is treated as a man's church, let us not wait to see God's work fully manifested. God is building His Church, and He leads us in His will, not ours.

At the beginning, our only love was Him. We thirsted for His presence. We could spend hours on our knees, meditating on the Word, without seeing the time pass. We didn't sing to be applauded, we simply wanted to pray. Today, when you are in His presence, you count the seconds.
3. The illusion of religious activism

Jesus warns us. One day some will stand before Him and say, “We have done miracles in your name, we have cast out demons in your name. » And He will answer them: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity. »

Iniquity also means abandoning one's first love. Iniquity is transforming the relationship into a simple ritual. It is loving to preach for the pleasure of gaining authority and being seen, rather than out of love for souls. Sometimes the desire to stand before people is stronger than the desire to see those people saved.
You fight to win souls, but you forget that your own life is itself a soul to be saved. The souls you want to win don't need you to take anyone else's life; They need you to be a role model first.
God is not just looking to use you to serve Him if, deep down, you are lost. Are you yourself saved? Is your life right before Him?

You're not a superhero. You are not the savior that Jesus sends to save the world in His place; you yourself have a vital need of the Savior. You must first save yourself before you want to save others.
4. Our responsibility: personal sanctification
In 2 Timothy chapter 2, verse 21, it is written:
“Nevertheless, the firm foundation of God stands, with these words as its seal: The Lord knows those who are his; and: Whoever calls the name of the Lord, let him depart from iniquity. »

Notice carefully what this text says: "Whoever calls the name of the Lord, let him depart..." It is not God who removes us from iniquity by force, it is our responsibility to move away from it. There are environments, habits and compromises that you need to remove yourself from.

At some point, you have to know how to stop and ask yourself: “Lord, where am I? What's wrong with me? » Stop blaming others by asking yourself: “What did someone do to me? » Instead, ask yourself: “What did I do wrong? Where did I go astray? Does my life honor God? »
The apostle Paul goes on to say:

“In a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earth; some are vessels of honor, and others are of vile use. If therefore anyone keeps himself pure by abstaining from these things, he will be a vessel of honor, sanctified, useful to his master, fit for every good work. »
Do you want to serve God? Do you want to be useful in His hands? Keep yourself pure.

The work doesn't start on others, it starts on yourself. Don't start by wanting to lead others; start by leading yourself. The power of God that heals and works through you must first be exercised in you.

If you are living in a mess and feel like everything is okay because God lets you, know that this is an extremely dangerous state. If you enjoy sin without feeling conviction, where has your spiritual sensitivity gone?

We cannot impart purity to others if we ourselves live in filth. We don't just transmit what we say, we transmit what we are. When you preach or serve, you share your spirit. Jesus said, “The prince of this world is coming, and there is nothing of him in me. » Can you say the same thing?
Abstaining from iniquity is not for God's sake, it is for your own good. God will remain God, but you need this sanctification to remain a useful vessel of honor in His hands.
5. Respect and fear of God
In the book of Malachi, chapter 1, verse 6, the Lord calls to us:
“A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, where is the honor due to me? If I am master, where is the fear that people have of me? says the LORD of hosts...
God doesn’t need people who just call Him “Father” with their lips. He needs people who demonstrate through their lives that He is truly their Father. And how do we show it? By honor.

Honor is expressed by the respect we give Him and by our obedience to His Word. The Lord tells us clearly: if you do not honor me, do not call me Father. When we say this name, we commit to respecting Him.
Of course, honoring God is not always easy. True honor comes through difficulty. It's when you don't want to do His will, but you do it anyway out of respect for His name.
Let's return to the fear of God. Let's put the sacred in its place.
Where has the fear we once had gone? When it came to passing on the Word, we spent weeks in prayer because we knew it was not a game, it was not a joke. We took the things of God seriously.
Today, we can spend the whole week in disorder, laughing and neglecting His presence, and come on Sunday to preach as if nothing had happened. Where has the fear of God gone?
Conclusion and appeal
In 2 Corinthians 13:5, the Word exhorts us:
“Examine yourselves whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. »

This post is not for you to save for anyone else. He's for you, he's for me. We have a great facility in examining others, in analyzing whether one preaches well or whether another is sincere. It's so easy to scrutinize others. But the Scripture tells us: examine yourself. Look at yourself in the mirror of the Word.

The apostle Paul said: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. » Leadership is not what you say, it's what you do. It’s leading the way by example. Do you want people to have fire for God? Do you have this fire yourself? How do you expect them to burn if they don't see fire in you?

When you are transformed, your words will naturally become powerful because people will see your message embodied in your own life. Preaching what we don't live is like a poorly styled hairdresser who claims to know how to beautify others. Who would trust him?
Finally, the apostle James gives us this loving warning in James 3:1:
“My brothers, let not many among you begin to teach, for you know that we will be judged more severely. »

Teaching and transmitting the Word is an immense responsibility. He who shows the way must himself take it. We can understand that a student does not understand the course, but we have difficulty accepting it from the teacher.
Let's not look for the title, look for the transformation. The impact of our message depends on the depth of our personal transformation.
Prayer
Let us pray together so that this word takes root in our lives:
Lord, let this word penetrate my heart. I want to return to my first love, Father. I want to rediscover the love of Your Word and the fear of what You are.

Forgive me if service has taken precedence over You, for You are the God of service. Forgive me if preaching has taken precedence over You, because it is You who inspires the message. Very often I have strayed from Your will and from my first love. Very often I examined others instead of examining myself. I read Your Word only to transmit it, and not to be personally edified and nourished by it.
Today, I question myself. I refuse to blame others. I want to save souls, but I remember that I myself am a soul who needs You. I want to be a servant, but first I want to be an obedient son.
Take me back to basics. I reposition You as the center of my life. I'm not a superhero, you're the hero. I am not the savior, You are the Savior, and I need You.

Restore me, Lord. Give me to preach by the example of my life. Remove from me any spiritual pride that would make me believe that Your messages are always for others and never for me. May Your Word transform me first.
In the name of Jesus, Amen.
